guide.title: A Dream Within a Dream — a guided reading and memorisation plan
guide.description: An unhurried reading of Edgar Allan Poe’s poem, with short passages, images, sound and gentle returns to the text.

metadata.chunkingStrategy: Passages within original stanzas; chunks of at most two lines. Read aloud and recall at your own pace, without scored exercises.

poem.title: A Dream Within a Dream
poem.author: Edgar Allan Poe
poem.text:
Take this kiss upon thy brow!
And, in parting from you now,
Thus much let me avow —
You are not wrong, who deem
That my days have been a dream;
Yet if Hope has flown away
In a night, or in a day,
In a vision, or in none,
Is it therefore the less gone?
All that we see or seem
Is but a dream within a dream.

I stand amid the roar
Of a surf-tormented shore,
And I hold within my hand
Grains of the golden sand —
How few! yet how they creep
Through my fingers to the deep,
While I weep — while I weep!
O, God! can I not grasp
Them with a tighter clasp?
O, God! can I not save
One from the pitiless wave?
Is all that we see or seem
But a dream within a dream?

metadata.edition: Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore reading text, based on the Flag of Our Union with minor changes from the Examiner proof-sheets. Keep thy brow, capital Hope, spaced em dashes and O, God! Two stanzas of 11 and 13 lines; learning groups do not create extra stanzas.

sessions.title: A parting voice
sessions.focusSummary: Begin with a kiss, an address and an unfinished thought.

pages.title: An invitation to read
pages.bodyMarkdown: Poe begins with a farewell and moves to a shore where sand escapes a hand. His questions about reality have a physical urgency. Avow means declare; deem means think or judge. We will linger with short passages inside the poem’s two unequal stanzas, keeping their original divisions intact. Let the repeated sounds help you hear where you are.

pages.title: Stay with these lines
pages.bodyMarkdown: Read the passage aloud, following the sentence through the line endings. Pause over an image or sound that draws your attention.

pages.title: A parting voice
pages.bodyMarkdown: The first three lines share a rhyme, holding the farewell together. The fourth opens a new thought that will continue into the next passage: these learning pauses are not new stanzas. Thy means your. Try speaking the lines to one imagined listener, letting the dash after avow prepare the declaration. The voice is intimate even before it begins to question what can be known.

pages.title: Let the words return
pages.bodyMarkdown: Hold the scene in mind and look away from the words. Try saying one or two lines, then return to the text wherever you need it. Join the passage together at a comfortable pace.

pages.title: A moment to linger
pages.prompt: What tone does the opening kiss give to the declaration that follows?

pages.title: A place to pause
pages.bodyMarkdown: You can leave the passage here for a while. If an image or a sound stays with you, let it. Return whenever you would like to hear how the next lines continue the thought.

pages.title: If Hope has flown
pages.bodyMarkdown: The first line completes the thought begun in the previous passage. Then Yet introduces a qualification. Night and day, vision and its absence: the speaker tries out alternatives, but the sentence has not reached its question. Listen for the paired rhymes as you keep the thought moving. Hope is capitalised in this edition. You can hear it almost as something living that has departed.

pages.title: A claim about dreaming
pages.bodyMarkdown: The opening question asks whether the manner of losing Hope makes the loss any less real. The final two lines appear to offer a firm statement, held together by seem and dream. Give the full stop its space. Then read the eleven-line stanza as one movement, from a parting gesture through uncertainty to a declaration. Notice whether the firmness sounds convincing to you.

pages.title: At the shore
pages.bodyMarkdown: The setting changes abruptly. Roar and shore bring the surf into the sound of the poem; hand and sand turn attention to something small enough to hold. Picture the scene before trying to remember the wording. The dash at the end leaves the gesture unfinished. The poem has moved from an idea about experience to an experience we can almost feel in the palm.

pages.title: Through the fingers
pages.bodyMarkdown: The grains are few, but their loss seems unstoppable. Creep suggests a slow movement even within the pressure of the surf. The repeated weeping interrupts the description with a voice in distress. In this edition, the appeal begins O, God! Keep the comma as a small vocal hesitation if it helps. Its unfinished question leads into the next passage, rather than ending here.

pages.title: A question returns
pages.bodyMarkdown: Clasp answers grasp across the learning boundary. Then a second appeal narrows the wish to saving even one grain. The poem’s earlier statement returns as a question, with Is at its beginning. Let that change be audible without deciding what answer the poem requires. Read the whole second stanza, then the poem from the beginning. Familiar words may feel less secure when they return.

pages.bodyMarkdown: Let the poem rest for now. A phrase may return later, or you may want to read it aloud again with a different emphasis. Familiarity can grow through small, unhurried returns.
